# Cooling the City: How Urban Design Can Tame Summer Heat

Every summer, cities become furnaces. Concrete and asphalt absorb sunlight all day and release it slowly at night, so urban temperatures routinely run five to ten degrees Fahrenheit hotter than surrounding countryside—a phenomenon known as the urban heat island effect. This gap matters more than it might seem. Extreme heat kills more Americans annually than hurricanes, floods, and tornadoes combined, and the burden falls hardest on the elderly, the poor, and those without air conditioning. As climate change makes heat waves longer and more intense, the question of how cities can stay livable in summer has moved from an aesthetic concern to a matter of public health. The good news is that cities have real tools: trees, smarter street design, cooler housing, and better transit. The complication is that each of these tools involves tradeoffs, and residents do not share the costs and benefits equally.

## The Humble Power of Trees

Trees are the most straightforward and cost-effective weapon against urban heat. A mature shade tree can lower surface temperatures beneath its canopy by twenty to forty degrees Fahrenheit, and through evapotranspiration—the process by which leaves release water vapor—it cools the surrounding air as well.
